title: As you sow
hook: as the seed is sown, so is the fruit reaped (SN 11.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kamma, a deed, made in the mind by intention. Your line: the half-second before the act.

Long ago, the Buddha says, a group of gentle seers lived in leaf huts by the sea. War was coming, the gods on one side and the asuras, the titans, on the other, and the seers were afraid the titans would harm them. So they went to the titans' king, a fearsome lord named Sambara, and asked him for one thing: a promise of safety. He laughed at them. No safety for you, he said. I give you fear instead. What the seers said back is a picture any farmer knows.
screen: `LEAF HUTS BY THE SEA.` → `A PROMISE OF SAFETY, PLEASE.` → `NO. I GIVE YOU FEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's their answer, close to the Pali. You give us fear when we ask for safety. Then let fear be yours, without end. As the seed that's sown, so is the fruit that's reaped. The one who does good reaps good; the one who does evil reaps evil. You've planted this seed, friend; you'll taste its fruit. Then the seers vanish. And that night, the sutta says, Sambara wakes in terror three times. Two things in this strange little story are worth noticing. First, the seers do wish him endless fear, but they don't lift a hand to bring it. They point to something they trust is already true: a seed grows into its own kind of plant. Plant fear, and fear is what comes up. Nobody has to deliver it. Second, the fruit can begin sooner than you'd think. Sambara doesn't wait a lifetime. The same night, the fear he handed out is in his own bed. That's the farmer's view of kamma. Yesterday said the deed is the intention. Today says the intention is a seed. Seeds don't sprout on demand; some come up in a season, some take years, and the suttas say kamma can ripen in this life or later ones. But no farmer plants chilies and expects to pull up melons. Pali talks about kamma's phala, its fruit, and its vipāka, its ripening: the language of an orchard.
screen: `THEN LET FEAR BE YOURS.` · `A SEED GROWS ITS OWN KIND.` · `THE SAME NIGHT, THREE TIMES.` · `PHALA AND VIPĀKA: FRUIT, RIPENING.` · then, large: `AS YOU SOW.`

segments.voice: Picture today as a field you've been walking through, scattering seeds without looking: a sharp reply, a kind note, an hour of scrolling, a promise kept. Just notice what's been planted so far, without grading it. Then let one good seed come to mind, a thank-you, a meal shared, five minutes of full attention, and feel its weight.
Phala, fruit. The seers' line in the Connected Discourses: as the seed that's sown, so is the fruit that's reaped.
Your line: chilies don't grow into melons. What you plant is, sooner or later, what you'll be eating. Day three hundred seventy-three, planted.

howItsDone: Buddhists often speak of good deeds as planting seeds of merit, and many make small daily offerings or acts of generosity with that image in mind.

fork.reveal: in SN 11.10 the seers answer that he will reap what he has sown, then vanish; that night Sambara wakes in terror three times.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit phala: fruit, the word for what a deed bears.

trapdoor: what you thought: you reap what you sow is a threat.
what it means: a seed grows its own kind: what you plant in intention comes up as its fruit.
what a scholar hears: the verse in SN 11.10 runs yādisaṃ vapate bījaṃ, tādisaṃ harate phalaṃ, spoken by seers to a titan king, and the story is set inside the old war of gods and asuras.

chat.says: If someone does harm, does somebody have to punish them for it to come back?
options: No one has to; as the seers said, a seed grows its own fruit.
Yes, the gods hand out each result, as a reward or a punishment.
Nothing comes back at all; deeds simply vanish once they are done.
chat.meaning: The seers wish Sambara fear but do nothing to bring it: as the seed that's sown, so the fruit that's reaped. That same night, he wakes in terror.

asuras.meaning: titans who war with the gods in the old stories

Sambara.meaning: the titans' king, who gave the seers fear

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 11.10 (Samuddaka Sutta, the seers by the ocean)

notes: SN 11.10 paraphrased: seers by the ocean, Sambara the asura lord refuses safety and gives fear; seers reply with the seed verse and vanish; Sambara is alarmed three times in the night. Confirm details.
Pali verse given from memory (yādisaṃ vapate bījaṃ, tādisaṃ harate phalaṃ; kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpakaṃ): please confirm.
'The suttas say kamma can ripen in this life or later ones' (e.g. AN 6.63): general statement.
Mrs Rhys Davids's 1917 Kindred Sayings I translation of this verse was not quoted because its exact wording could not be confirmed.
